Augustin-Jean Fresnel was a French civil engineer and physicist. Fresnel pioneered in optics and did much to establish the wave theory of light advanced by English physicist Thomas young. Fresnel presented his work on diffractionin 1819. A mathematician Simeon-Denis Poisson (a prominent advocate of Newton’s corpuscular model of light) pointed out that Fresnel’s model predicted a different result: when a parallel beam of light falls on a small spherical obstacle, there will be a bright spot at the centre of the circular shadow. The spot was nearly as bright as if the obstacle was not there at all. An experiment performed by the French physicist Aragoand validated that spot (subsequently called Poisson’s spot).

18.1 Introduction The dispersion of light is an important phenomenon in the field of optics, which provides the spectrum of colors that forms the essence of our visual world. When white light encounters a medium like a prism or a droplet of water, its composite wavelengths undergo a mesmerizing transformation, and give an array of colors ranging from violet to red, each representing a unique wavelength of light. This phenomenon is known as dispersion, and it was famously demonstrated by Isaac Newton in the 17th century. The study of dispersion explores the secrets behind rainbows, colour spectrum from prisms, and a number of natural phenomena.

18.2 Dispersion of light A

When a beam of white light falls on the refracting face of a prism, it splits into seven colours as shown in figure 18.1. Those seven colours are violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, and red. The band of seven colours obtained on the screen is called the spectrum of white light. The phenomenon is called the dispersion of light. Therefore, dispersion of light is defined as the phenomenon of splitting white light into its constituent colors. The formation of a rainbow is an example of the dispersion of light.

18.3 Cause of Dispersion The refractive index of a medium is highly colour dependent. It is inversely proportional to the wave length of the light (from Cauchy’s empirical relation = A+ 2 B + 4 c + ......). Since, the λλ wave length of orange light is smaller than that of red light, the refractive index of red colour r is less than that of orange colour o. Similarly, the refractive index of yellow light is less than that of orange light and so on. Therefore from the relation  = A ( – 1), v>i>b>g>y>o>r. That is different colour of light deviate along different directions with different values of angle of deviation. Therefore, when white light is incident on a refracting face of a prism, different colours are refracted through different angles. As a result, a white light splits and dispersion takes place.

Results of dispersion of light a. Rainbow The natural phenomenon of dispersion of light is the dispersion of sunlight in the sky which gives a rainbow formation. Rainbow is a natural spectrum which is seen in the sky. During rainfall, a rain drop behaves as a dispersive medium like a prism, and the sky acts as screen so that at a particular and suitable angle of incidence, a white ray of light incident on rain drop splits into its seven constituent colours, and a rainbow is seen in the sky.

b. Blue colour of sky

The sky looks blue due to the dispersion of light followed by scattering. When sunlight passes through the atmosphere it suffers dispersion. Also,it suffers scattering from dust particles and air molecules. According to Rayleigh empirical formula of scatterin is 1 g (scattering intensity  4 ). Red light scatters least, λ and blue light scatters most. The blue colour, which scatters most, covers the sky. Due to this the sky seems blue. Blue sky due to dispersion]

c. Sun appears red during Sunrise and Sun-set The Sun light suffers dispersion during its long travel through the atmosphere. During sunrise or sunset, when the Sun is close to the horizon, the light must travel a longer distance through the atmosphere than it does when the Sun is overhead. This results in comparatively more scattering of light. Red colour scatters the least, and becomes capable to reach our eyes, but other colours scatter away. Hence, during sunset and sunrise the sun appears red.
